Text | Er Mu

Editors | Er Mu, Fanyu Meng

A road that sings?!

What’s that supposed to mean?

That the road sings all by itself?

Driving on an ordinary road, we hear a jumble of humming and droning. But on certain special roads, the road surface itself plays a rhythm, or even a tune.

Let’s go straight to the video and hear it for ourselves!

Wow~ Roads like this really exist, and they don’t sound half bad. It’s a big world out there, full of wonders.

So is this some marvel of nature?

No, it’s a triumph of human ingenuity.

What romantic road engineers!

Nope. Your no-nonsense engineer would never dream of it; they just make sure the road is built to spec.

The idea came from two Danish artists, Steen Krarup Jensen and Jakob Freud-Magnus.

Only free-spirited artists would come up with something this gloriously “pointless.”

Back in 1995, the two of them built the world’s first singing road in Gylling, Denmark, and even gave it a name of its own: the Asphaltophone.

How did they do it? By laying raised road markers across the road at regular intervals. So easy! It really is that simple.

Take a look at their video; you can skip straight to 1:30.

(Danish sounds a lot like German!)

Why does a pattern of road markers produce a melody when cars drive over it?

Each time a vehicle crosses a row of raised markers, it produces an impact. Take middle C (C4) as an example: its frequency is 264 Hz, meaning 264 vibrations per second. At a speed of 60 km/h, the rows of markers need to be 6.3 cm apart. For a given speed, each note corresponds to one spacing, so by varying the spacing of the markers along the direction of travel, you can compose music on the road.

You may have noticed that all this assumes a fixed speed. Turn it around: once the raised markers are laid, the spacing really is fixed, so to hear the intended melody you have to drive at the speed it was designed for. Many singing roads have signs ahead telling drivers the target speed.

After Denmark, other countries built singing roads of their own, though not always for the same reasons. Here’s a quick roundup:

Denmark

The Danes built their singing road because their artists let their imaginations soar. Their tune is in F major.

Hungary

The video at the start of this article shows Hungary’s singing road. It was built in memory of Cipő, the lead singer of Republic, one of the country’s best-loved bands, and lies on Route 67 between Mernyeszentmiklós and Mernye. The tune, fittingly, is the band’s signature song, “Route 67.”

South Korea

In Anyang, between Seoul and Suwon, the local road authority also built a singing road. The original aim was to reduce accidents. The road is an S-bend, and drivers who have been at the wheel for hours tend to get drowsy and crash; a burst of music from the road surface wakes them up. The tune is the nursery rhyme “Mary Had a Little Lamb.” Though it was built to keep drivers awake, it gradually turned into a tourist hotspot.

Japan

Unlike South Korea, which ended up with a tourist attraction by happy accident, Japan builds these roads mainly to draw visitors and boost tourism. The Japanese also seem keener on the idea than anyone else: by one count, Japan has as many as 35 singing roads, plus a “music tunnel.” The tunes include plenty of pop songs, and one road even plays Beethoven’s “Ode to Joy.”

United States

The US has two fairly well-known roads of this kind. One is in Lancaster, California, built by Honda to promote its Civic. It was completed on Avenue K on September 5, 2008, but after complaints from local residents it was removed and rebuilt on Avenue G, five kilometers away, reopening on October 15 that year. The tune is the William Tell Overture. As if that weren’t bad luck enough, the road wasn’t built quite right and the tune is a little off-key, reportedly because the spacing of the grooves was miscalculated. (Somebody dock that engineer’s lunch!!!) Have a listen below: it really doesn’t sound good, and it’s rather grating.

The other, slightly better one is on the famous Route 66, near Albuquerque, New Mexico. Funded by the National Geographic Society, it was completed in 2014. Much like the one in Anyang, it was built mainly to remind drivers not to speed and to prevent accidents. The tune is “America the Beautiful.”

China

Beijing’s Fengtai District has a singing road too, on Qianling Mountain, completed in 2016. Drive at 40 km/h and you’ll hear the melody of “Ode to the Motherland.” It, too, was designed mainly to remind drivers not to speed and to drive safely. And since it is the only way into the Qianling Mountain scenic area, it also helps draw tourists. It isn’t China’s first musical road, though. Back in 2013, the city of Changge in Henan province built China’s first musical road surface, which plays “March of the Volunteers” (the national anthem) and “Jasmine Flower.” In 2014, Yantai in Shandong province built two more, playing the “Toreador Song” from Carmen and “Ode to Joy.”

Most musical roads don’t actually sound all that musical, but the idea is a lovely one. It’s just a bit hard on the tires.

So if you get the chance, would you take a drive to hear one for yourself?
